slides.title: The one idea: tokens read from each other
slides.summary: Attention lets each token gather information from the other tokens it needs, so words take on meaning from their context.
body: After embedding, each token's vector ignores its surroundings. "Bank" has the same vector in "river bank" and "bank account". To understand text, a token has to look at its neighbours.
Attention is how it does that. Each token builds a new, context-aware vector by pulling in information from the other tokens that matter to it.
Every token plays three roles at once:

ul: Query: what this token is looking for. Something like "I'm an adjective; which noun do I describe?"
Key: what this token offers, used for matching. "I'm a noun."
Value: the information this token hands over if it's chosen.

body: Each query is compared with every key. Good matches get large weights, and the token's new vector is a weighted blend of the matching values.

body.note: A database lookup returns the one row whose key equals your query. Attention returns a blend of every row, weighted by how well each key matches. Because nothing is all-or-nothing, the whole thing can be learned by gradual adjustment.

body: The next four slides compute this step by step on "I am learning artificial", with real numbers.

slides.title: Step 1: project into Q, K, V
slides.summary: Three learned matrices turn each token's vector into a query, a key and a value.
body: Each token's vector x is multiplied by three different learned weight matrices, giving three new vectors per token:

ul: Q = x·Wq: the query. What am I looking for?
K = x·Wk: the key. What do I contain?
V = x·Wv: the value. What will I hand over if picked?

body: These are ordinary matrix multiplications, the "many dot products at once" operation from The big picture. Nobody designs Wq, Wk and Wv by hand. Training adjusts them until the queries and keys pick out useful relationships.
To keep the numbers readable, each token here has 4 numbers (d_model = 4) and each Q, K or V vector has 3 (d_head = 3). Real models use thousands and 64–128 respectively.

body.note: Each row of the Q table is one token's query vector. Green cells are positive numbers, red cells negative, and stronger colour means a larger magnitude.

code: q, k, v = Wq(x), Wk(x), Wv(x)    # each [B, n, d_head]

slides.title: Step 2: score every pair
slides.summary: Every query is compared with every key using a dot product, giving a grid of relevance scores.
body: Now compare every query with every key using a dot product. For 4 tokens that gives a 4 × 4 grid of scores, written S = Q·Kᵀ. (Kᵀ is K transposed, flipped on its side so the multiplication lines up.)
Read the grid one row at a time. Row i says how relevant each token is to token i. A high score means token i's query matches that token's key well.

Dot products of long vectors produce big numbers. Big scores make the next step (softmax) put almost all the weight on a single token, and then training barely learns. Dividing by the square root of the vector length, here √3, keeps the scores in a comfortable range.

body.note: The grid has one entry for every pair of tokens, so n tokens give n² entries. Double the text length and you get four times the work. That's where attention's famous O(n²) cost comes from.

slides.title: Step 3: the causal mask
slides.summary: A mask stops each token looking at later tokens. That's what makes next-token training work.
body: GPT, Claude, Llama and other chat models are decoder-only models trained to predict the next token. If a position could see the token after it, predicting it would be trivial: the model would just copy the answer.
So every score above the diagonal, where a token would look at a later token, is set to −∞ (minus infinity). In the next step those become exactly 0: no attention to the future.

There's a big bonus. Since no token can see ahead, one pass over a training sentence trains every position at once: position 1 predicts token 2, position 2 predicts token 3, and so on, all in parallel.

Encoder models like BERT, used for classification and search embeddings, skip the mask and look both ways. That's great for understanding a complete sentence, but they can't generate text one token at a time. Toggle the mask to compare.

slides.title: Step 4: softmax, then blend the values
slides.summary: Softmax turns each row of scores into weights that add up to 1, and the output is the matching blend of values.
body: Each row of scores becomes attention weights through softmax: raise e (≈ 2.718) to the power of each score, then divide each result by their total. The weights are all positive and add up to 1, like percentages.

body.note: Scores [2, 1, 0] become e² ≈ 7.39, e¹ ≈ 2.72 and e⁰ = 1, which total 11.11. The weights are 0.67, 0.24 and 0.09. The biggest score gets the most weight, but the others still get some. A masked score of −∞ becomes e<sup>−∞</sup> = 0.

body: Each token's output is then the weighted sum of all value vectors: out = softmax(S)·V. If "artificial" puts 36% of its weight on "learning", then 36% of its new vector comes from the value of "learning".
Pick a query row on the right to see where that token looks and what it gets back.

body.note: That's all of attention: compare (Q·K), normalise (softmax), blend (·V). The rest of this chapter is about doing it many times in parallel, and doing it fast.

slides.title: Multi-head attention
slides.summary: Models run many small attention operations side by side, so each can track a different kind of relationship.
body: A single attention pattern has to choose where to look. But a token often needs several kinds of information at once: the previous word, the subject of the sentence, a matching bracket far back in some code.

So models run h attention heads in parallel, each with its own Wq, Wk and Wv. To keep the cost the same, each head works with smaller vectors: d_head = d_model / h. A model with d_model = 4,096 and 32 heads gives each head 128 numbers.
Each head produces its own output. These are joined end to end (concatenated) and mixed together by one more learned matrix, Wo.

body.note: A team reading the same document, each person told to look for something different, who then pool their notes.

body: Researchers who study model internals (interpretability) find heads that specialise. The four patterns on the right are simplified versions of common ones. The first-token pattern is real and has a name, an attention sink: a place where heads park their weight when nothing else is relevant.
code: q = q.view(B, n, h, d_head).transpose(1, 2)  # [B, h, n, d_head]
out = attention(q, k, v)                     # per head

slides.title: The cost of attention, and the fixes
slides.summary: Attention's work grows with the square of the text length, and a few key tricks keep it manageable.
body: The score grid has n² entries for every head in every layer. At 1,000 tokens that's a million scores per head. At a million tokens it's a trillion. Drag the slider to watch it explode.
Three widely used fixes:

ul: FlashAttention computes exactly the same result, but in small tiles that fit in the GPU's fast on-chip memory, so the full grid is never written out. Same maths, far less slow memory traffic. It's now the default in major frameworks.
Grouped-query attention (GQA): several query heads share one set of key and value heads. Quality stays close, and the KV cache (see Output & inference) shrinks several times over.
Sliding-window and sparse attention: some layers only look back a fixed distance, or at selected positions, instead of at everything.

body.note: This is why long context is expensive. Even with these tricks, a 200,000-token prompt costs far more compute and memory than a 2,000-token one.
